messages.content:
Compute the largest positive integer \( n \) such that

\[
n \text{ divides } (\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor)!^{n!} + 450.
\]

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let

\[
m=\lfloor \sqrt n\rfloor,\qquad A=m!.
\]

We need

\[
n\mid A^{n!}+450.
\]

Let \(p\) be a prime divisor of \(n\), and write \(e=v_p(n)\).

---

### 1. Primes \(p\le m\)

If \(p\le m\), then \(p\mid A\). Hence

\[
v_p(A^{n!})=n!v_p(A)\ge n!\ge n\ge e,
\]

so

\[
A^{n!}\equiv 0 \pmod{p^e}.
\]

Since \(n\mid A^{n!}+450\), we must also have

\[
p^e\mid 450.
\]

Because

\[
450=2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2,
\]

any prime \(p\le m\) dividing \(n\) must be one of \(2,3,5\), with exponent at most \(1,2,2\), respectively. Thus the part of \(n\) composed of primes \(\le m\) divides \(450\).

---

### 2. Primes \(p>m\)

If \(p>m\), then \(p\nmid A\). Also \(p^2>n\), since otherwise \(\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor\ge p\), contradiction. So \(p\) appears to the first power.

Because \(p\mid n\), we have \(p-1\le n\), so \(p-1\mid n!\). By Fermat’s little theorem,

\[
A^{n!}\equiv 1 \pmod p.
\]

Thus

\[
A^{n!}+450\equiv 1+450=451 \pmod p.
\]

Therefore \(p\mid 451\). Since

\[
451=11\cdot 41,
\]

the only possible prime divisor of \(n\) larger than \(m\) is \(11\) or \(41\).

There can be at most one such prime, because two primes larger than \(m\) would multiply to at least \((m+1)^2>n\).

So \(n\) has the form

\[
n=d
\]

or

\[
n=qd,
\]

where \(q\in\{11,41\}\) and \(d\mid 450\).

If \(q>1\), then \(q>m=\lfloor\sqrt{qd}\rfloor\), so

\[
q^2>qd\implies q>d.
\]

Thus \(d\) must be a divisor of \(450\) smaller than \(q\).

- If \(q=11\), then \(d<11\), so \(d\le 10\), giving \(n\le 110\).
- If \(q=41\), then \(d<41\). The largest divisor of \(450\) below \(41\) is \(30\), giving \(n\le 41\cdot 30=1230\).
- If there is no such \(q\), then \(n=d\le 450\).

Therefore every solution satisfies

\[
n\le 1230.
\]

---

### 3. Check \(n=1230\)

Let

\[
n=1230=2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 41.
\]

Then

\[
\lfloor\sqrt{1230}\rfloor=35,
\]

since \(35^2=1225<1230<1296=36^2\).

Now \(35!\) is divisible by \(30\), and \(450=15\cdot 30\), so

\[
35!^{1230!}+450\equiv 0\pmod{30}.
\]

Also, \(41\nmid 35!\), and \(40\mid 1230!\). Hence by Fermat’s little theorem,

\[
35!^{1230!}\equiv 1\pmod{41}.
\]

Since \(450\equiv -1\pmod{41}\),

\[
35!^{1230!}+450\equiv 1-1=0\pmod{41}.
\]

Because \(\gcd(30,41)=1\), we get

\[
1230\mid 35!^{1230!}+450.
\]

Thus the largest possible \(n\) is

\[
\boxed{1230}
\]
